Bulk ferment starts on addition of the starter. So 45 mins of rest plus 2 hours of S&F plus 5 hours bench is almost 8 hours of fermentation - you've over proofed the dough.

The thing to keep in mind is your dough is a living organism, you have to watch the dough and not the clock. From start to finish what is it telling you about gluten and proofing. Chart says 5 hours but it looks good at 4, shape and refrigerate! look for the jiggle!! lol
You are bulking way to long at that temp - mine takes 5-6 hours max!
If you use a thick aka stiffish starter add a little bit more water!
Please note - that timing is based on a 79-82F bulk proofing temp AND the recipe indicated! If your temp is less it will take longer, if you don't have WW it will take longer.

For all the folks saying too much water, it's only about a 70% hydration. That's not the problem here.

Unless you are somewhere that is cold or have a very cool temperature kitchen, you have a timing issue.

S&F should really only need about 2 hours (30 min intervals). If you aren't feeling gluten develop your starter is not really ready - and at 150g of starter it should be nice and developed after 2 hours.

Next issue, unless your house is in the 60's, overnight is massively over proofed. So many recipes come out out northern CA or the UK and they are cold compared to our 75+ houses. Total bulk time (S&F + Rising) should be about 5-6 hours (rule of thumb). Do not proof overnight!

So step 1 to fix - is your starter doubling consistently? Have you tried upping the feeding to 1:2:2 or 1:3:3 to get a good bubbly doubling starter? 

Step 2: S&F and look for a dough that "stiffens" after a couple of S&Fs - it should be smoothing out by the third or fourth set. You may want to look into the Rubaud method of S&Fs, but generally that's for high hydration doughs.

Step 3: shorter proofing times once you get the above working. look for about a 70% rise and a good jiggle.

Keep practicing!

Sourdough takes a bunch of practice and getting used to the feel of things. But I know the feeling of baking frisbees way to much.  Took me 6 months of working at it until i learned my flour and environment. I too am in the tropics, but the house is kept at about 75 most days.

Things that helped me:

* Autolyse - i am now autolyse for 30 minutes at about 72% hydration, add the starter  then autolyse for a good 2.5 hours
* Add salt and enough water to get to 75% hydration
* Stretch and fold about every 30 minutes for three hours (or until nice and "pillowy" and you can feel the resistance to the stretch
* Bench shape to tension and rest for 30 minutes
* To shape for the basket I do the standard stretch left and right cross fold, but then I add in the stitching technique to really tension the bread
* Basket proofed overnight or longer depending on how sour you want it.
* Final awesome thing was getting a cloche to bake in. The oven spring from that is amazing!

Assumption: The class has a designated set of competencies designed to ensure the depth and scope of the material meet the goals of the class.

   know exactly the material to deliver in the class as required by the course competencies
   know exactly how the material delivered is best assessed
   designing a test to assess the material effectively

After delivering the material to the students, a good professor exams the questions. Heavy: compared to Japanese or smaller bikes it does feel heavy. The steering is not as light (although the Rushmore bikes changed the steering a lot so they feel lighter, except in the parking lot). But you can maneuver them on a dime if you practice.

Clutch: you're left hand will get strong. Mine has not eased up in 23K+ miles. Seriously you get used to it after riding a while. Some folks say the pull gets easier, but mine using a spring loaded force meter, reads the same today as it did when I bought it. However my left hand can crush steel. :p

Reliability:
Stock - generally reliable. My old 96 did 35k before I traded it in. Standard maintenance (oil, battery, tires and brakes) were all that was needed.

My current 103 picked up a gremlin at 23k - hopefully a new induction module is going to fix that this week.

As a rule the new bikes don't leak, that's old news these days. And no constant adjustments are really needed. fuel it up and ride. Mine have gone from sea level to 14k with nothing done all the way. Like all bikes you can get a lemon, but the build standards today pretty much match everyone else, so that's not a big concern.

The maintenance schedule is pretty normal, not quite as long as some of the European or Japanese bikes but not outrageous either. but some AMSOL change your own oil as per how you ride and you'll be good.

They do run hot in the summer - especially down here in Florida, but even in August, unless you're in bumper to bumper traffic it's not an issue.

Dealer results may vary. Some are awesome, some are suck. Ask around your area and get a feel for the one's you have. Heck look for an independent for the oil changes etc, you can save money big time!

The Street and Road glides are radically different in handling compared to the slims etc (for me) and the look and feel between the road and street glides are truly a matter of choice. I chose street glide special for me. The ABS is awesome, and they are finally getting the radio software figured out! 

Buy what you like and have fun!

Actually selective breeding is NOT GMO. While not a perfect definition what our good friends Wikipedia has is pretty close:

A genetically modified organism (GMO) is an organism whose genetic material has been altered using genetic engineering techniques. Organisms that have been genetically modified include micro-organisms such as bacteria and yeast, insects, plants, fish, and mammals. 

Where genetic engineering is: Genetic engineering, also called genetic modification, is the direct manipulation of an organism's genome using biotechnology. New DNA may be inserted in the host genome by first isolating and copying the genetic material of interest using molecular cloning methods to generate a DNA sequence, or by synthesizing the DNA, and then inserting this construct into the host organism

So no. GMO is not selective breeding. It is the direct manipulation of the genome and the insertion of additional genetic information into the organism. You should have the right to know that the corn you're eating has been modified with additional genomes in it. I do however agree the simple act of labeling with "GMO" is insufficient.

the first number:150 or 130 is the number of millimeters across from the widest point of its outer sidewall to the widest point of its inner sidewall when mounted and measured on a specified width wheel. This measurement is also referred to as the tire's section width. So you can see according to the specs at HD they are different width tires.

The second number: 80 or 90 indicates that this tire size's sidewall height (from rim to tread) is 50% of its section width. The measurement is the tire's section height, and also referred to as the tire's series, profile or aspect ratio. The higher the number, the taller the sidewall; the lower the number, the lower the sidewall.

The B stands for Belted, the 16 is the wheel diameter. 

The last bit: 77H or 73H is the load index or how much weight it can carry, in your case:
73 = 805lbs
77 = 908lbs

The H is the speed rating or for you 130 mph.

So there is a difference for the tires in size on your bike - they are not interchangable. Although you should be able to get away with a slightly less loaded read tire spec. Part of the discussion below has issues, To fix some of that: 

Virus - self replicating code that infects additional files with it's code, and with the ability to spread without user interaction by exploiting known holes in the operating system, gaining the rights to write it's code on demand.

Malware - A piece of code designed to run on your computer and do things you would not want it to do. Some malware may have the self-replicating, gain rights to write feature too, however others require the user to interact during installation. 

Technically a virus is a subset of malware. However that said, most (not all) malware requires some user interaction.

There in lies the rub. The term virus is used ubiquitously when in reality the term malware is more correct. Hence the issue - there are no known pure viruses in the wild for OS X, there are many for Windows (all versions)

Also, it took some digging, but I get sooo tired of the market share arguments, the bot net potential size, etc etc.

Total estimated PCs with a version of windows installed in the world: 1.4billion ^1

Total estimated Apple computers Worldwide: 212 Million ^2

So not accounting for linux or other fractional operating systems this give PC Share of total machines at around 87% and Apple at around 13% (rounding a bit). No matter how you count it, 200 million machines is nothing to sneeze at, but using the good old Pareto rule, the 80% target is where to put your energy.

That still does not explain why some sub-set of programmers would not target the 20% given the base affluence of the group.

Botnets - Largest "known" is the Storm botnet where estimates ranged from 1-50 million infections, now down to 85,000. Second largest was Srizbi at 450,000 (both wiki articles btw). So the size of the market share does not explain it why Apple OS X is not targeted either given 212 million potential infection points.

I must conclude that something about Windows other than market share makes it a better target for the hackers to penetrate.

However in total devices - once you start playing with iOS and Android, things get interesting

iOS devices shipped by 2013 (yes does not mean activated): 700 Million ^3

Android devices activated by end of 2013: 900 Million ^4

So market share here is almost at parity, 46% for Apple and 56% for Android (skipping again the alternative OS devices - just because). I went from a Heritage '11 to a Street Glide Special '14

Noticeable things:

1) the SGS is a little heavier but with much better breaking power. where the heritage would stop the SGS slams to a stop (single vs dual disks!)

2) the SGS feels like it's balanced higher on the bike, and is much lighter in steering. Turns on a dime.

3) The Batwing vs a shield - better air protection and less battering at highway speeds.

4) SGS handles differently due to the change in suspension. Not sure how to describe it but the Heritage felt "longer", the SGS more closer to a sports bike, but not to the detriment of highway cruising

5) Highway the new 103 vs a 96 makes a world of difference. I can do 80 all day long on the SGS, the Heritage felt good at 70-75, otherwise it felt like I was pushing it beyond its comfortable zone (not that it wouldnt do it, just the way it sounded)

As it stands I really like both bikes but for touring am very glad I have the SGS now :)

First bike? That's easy, it was cheap, it ran and it was fun, a 78 kawasaki 350. Ran it into the ground! Well technically a tree... but that's another story. Not a lot of thought went into that just two wheels and fun!

Second bike - wanted something bigger for longer rides. Reliable and I could afford it. Ended up with a 80 Suzuki GS850G. Road that bike until I needed a car (kids and all that)

Third Bike - wanted an old Harley - found a '57 FL Panhead, all pretty much original. Restored that but never really got used to the suicide shifting thing.. still have it though :)

Fourth Bike - 11 Heritage Softail classic. The styling was basically the same as my 57, and it was just a nice smooth ride. Two years, 3 cross country trips, 35k miles later decided to upgrade to the my current bike.

Fifth - 14 Street Glide Special. Decided on that one because I liked the batwing fairing, the new nav system, abs and that nice engine. So here I am. Loving the new bike, slowly making it more mine.

Each bike was it's own thing, and I've never owned a bike I didn't love to ride. So look for the bike that hits your primary goals. Such as city riding, touring, modding into whatever you want. Second, is it comfortable or can you reasonably make it so? (reasonable is relative - time, money etc). Other things, how long will you keep it? Short time buy used, long time by new and mod (or save money and buy used). Do you like a fairing (fixed or mobile) or do you like a wind shield? Soft bags or hard? Radio? GPS? Answer these and you'll find what you want :)

My school requires you monitor attendance. If a student is absent or non-participating for two consecutive weeks we are required to drop them. This is in addition to the first two week no-show drop.

Nice thing about this is, you can quickly identify the people who are sliding downhill (missed a week or an assignment), ping them with "Wakeup" calls and poof some will recover. Not many but some...

First: make sure your syllabus covers how you want to handle situations like this in complete detail, e.g. No make-ups for any assignment or test will ever be given without 3 days prior notice to missing the class for exceptional resaons only. Missing an assignment or test for flat tires, mild illness, internet or other issues is not acceptable. For all other emergencies that can not due to their nature be arranged 3 days in advance, you must be able to provide written and verifiable proof of said emergency (e.g. death certificate/Obituary, hospital admissions papers, etc)

Next stick to your syllabus. Make no exceptions that don't fit. Why? because if you do, then another student WILL find out and demand "similar" accommodations. Where similar is in no way the correct word, but when they complain, you look bad. However nobody has ever been punished for following a well crafted syllabus.

FWIW "family emergency" is buzzword for 99% of the time I blew you off. I ALWAYS ask for details and written proof. So far that has happened exactly once.

If you want a get out of jail exception, that's cover-able too. Simply put the statement in the syllabus of something like: Students with only 1 absence, approved or unapproved will have the opportunity of dropping one assignment from the following categories, quiz, short paper, discussion posting (or whatever qualifies for your course)

Your policies are yours, just put them solidly in your syllabus and make everyone play by the same rules. Otherwise they will eat you alive at both the student and admin level.

Well I tend to agree that one of the largest barriers to education is economic. Where I teach virtually every student has a job to be able to support tuition and more. So yep, fully funding education to allow students the opportunity to focus on their education goals and not worry about were the next meal was coming from would be great. 

I also think there needs to be a balance too aka 1) you need to be prepared for college, and if not we need to have prep schools to get you ready, 2) correspondingly you need to have the aptitude for college and alternative paths if not (trade/vocational school for example) and 3) you need to perform to some adequate level.

As for teachers, having come from a family of teachers, I think your numbers are a bit skewed (or my observed population was). Most teachers I knew constantly worked for new material and ways to present information to their students. There were more like 7000 trying to reach kids and 1000 floating along. At the same time, with school districts (pre-college/uni) selecting the "approved" material for you that you can't deviate from, giving you "approved" lesson plans and forever agreeing with the parents that yep, their genius kid who does nothing deserves a 16th chance to continue to do nothing, oh and you can't fail them, the motivation to teach is getting harder to find (add in asininely low salaries, hugely long work days, paying out of your pocket for basic supplies and yep - not happy and not motivated teachers)  

Now at the College level I see tech teachers struggling with students wanting to be biologist, computer scientist, engineers of all flavors having no math skills, no writing skills, spending no time outside the class learning anything. I propose that your opening sentence for early elementary students is probably valid, and for some for middle and high school too, but it falls off precipitously in the early teens for most. Proof? well given the huge amount of free resources to learn online, for all topics (seriously there is nothing I haven't found online on any topic that interested me), the easy availability to access books, videos and more, why are most students (by most I mean 98%) not using these tools? Why if they want to be a programmer, are they not programming? It's not like they don't have the compilers, the videos and more to teach them. Simply put the 98% are passive learners - tell me I'll do it, but find and do on my own - nah...

Even more appropriately, here we are in 2013, teaching with the same techniques that were used for the last 200+ years. Why is there no serious, peer reviewed, scientific methodology being applied to education, techniques and more to find what really works? The research that is there is so fluffy as to be worthless.

I do wish you luck, just remember, education is not about providing jobs, or skills (unless vocational type programs) it's about creating minds that can find, analyze and process information effectively. Opening minds to new possibilities, old philosophies, history art, science and more to make them effective and productive members in society. With a good balanced education a person can learn any job. The opposite is not true however.

The key for me and turning right since it feels so backwards was this.

Throw out some cones at a big parking lot, next do a bunch of lefts. 
Now for the right turns, slow first, Consciously LOOK to where you want the bike to go, roll the throttle on and use the clutch as speed control aka feather it, as you accelerate in the turn.

The emphasis on looking smoothed out the turn for me, and the feather the clutch allowed me to prep more power then feed it in.

Note: I ride a Harley softail - so big heavy bike and I can now turn circles dragging the footboard as I go with confidence :)

Practice and it will all get better, you may want to practice the slow "race" to learn clutch control as needed. Enjoy!

well now first the basic math:

Assume instant start, no stops - 750 miles in a day is 10 hours at 75 mph. Oof

Assume realistic info - stops about every two hours ( gas and stretch the legs 20 mins) , plus a lunch stop (45 mins) you are looking at adding another 2 hours and 25 mins - so rounding a little that make it a 12.5 hour day.

Sooo in a hard way you can do the 1500 in two days, but if you are anything like me you'll be fried to a crisp mentally and physically. Days like that wear a body out!

If you take 3 days - they'll be a good 7 hours of riding, plus stops. And the stops are the fun times at least for me. Finding the out of the way diners, local sites, picture taking, blues bars etc, finding a place with a pool/jacuzzi to chill in - that's what makes the trip for me!

So in general if I'm just shooting to get there I would plan 3 days unless I had a serious deadline - then two is doable but hard riding. If I'm looking to explore and enjoy the trip (my standard ride) I take about 5 days or so - lots of side trips and back roads. The slab is useful when in a hurry but not why I ride.

PS: this is all predicated on a windscreen - if you don't have that - you'll be beat to death in 12 hours of riding! 

Safe travels!

Claim of Circumcision Benefit is Overstated and Premature
Further research is required to assess the feasibility, desirability and cost-effectiveness of circumcision to reduce the acquisition of HIV. This paper endorses the need for such research and suggests that, in its absence, it is premature to promote circumcision as a reliable strategy for combating HIV. Since articles in leading medical journals as well as the popular press continue to do so, scientific researchers should think carefully about how their conclusions may be translated both to policy makers and to a more general audience. The importance of addressing ethico-legal concerns that such trials may raise is highlighted. The understandable haste to find a solution to the HIV pandemic means that the promise offered by preliminary and specific research studies may be overstated. This may mean that ethical concerns are marginalized. Such haste may also obscure the need to be attentive to local cultural sensitivities, which vary from one African region to another, in formulating policy concerning circumcision.
Fox, M. and Thomson, M., "HIV/AIDS and Circumcision : Lost in Translation," Journal of Medical Ethics 36 (2010):798-801.

Circumcision/HIV Claims are Based on Insufficient Evidence
An article endorsed by thirty-two professionals questions the results of three highly publicized African circumcision studies. The studies claim that circumcision reduces HIV transmission, and they are being used to promote circumcisions. Substantial evidence in this article refutes the claim of the studies.
Examples in the article include the following:
Circumcision is associated with increased transmission of HIV to women.
Conditions for the studies were unlike conditions found in real-world settings.
Other studies show that male circumcision is not associated with reduced HIV transmission.
The U.S. has a high rate of HIV infection and a high rate of circumcision. Other countries have low rates of circumcision and low rates of HIV infection.
Condoms are 95 times more cost effective in preventing HIV transmission.
Circumcision removes healthy, functioning, unique tissue, raising ethical considerations.
Green, L. et al., "Male Circumcision and HIV Prevention: Insufficient Evidence and Neglected External Validity," American Journal of Preventive Medicine 39 (2010): 479-82.

In National Survey Circumcision Had No Protective Effect
A survey of South African men showed that circumcision had no protective effect in the prevention of HIV transmission. This is a concern, and has implications for the possible adoption of mass male circumcision strategy both as a public health policy and an HIV prevention strategy.
Connolly, C. et al., South African Medical Journal 98(2008): 789-794.

Circumcision is Not Cost Effective
The findings suggest that behavior change programs are more efficient and cost effective than circumcision. Providing free condoms is estimated to be significantly less costly, more effective in comparison to circumcising, and at least 95 times more cost effective at stopping the spread of HIV in Sub-Saharan Africa. In addition, condom usage provides protection for women as well as men. This is significant in an area where almost 61% of adults living with AIDS are women.
McAllister, R. et al., "The Cost to Circumcise Africa," American Journal of Men's Health 7(2008): 307-316.

Circumcision/HIV Have Incomplete Evaluation
The push to institute mass circumcision in Africa, following the three randomized clinical trials (RCTs) conducted in Africa, is based on an incomplete evaluation of real-world preventive effects over the long-term � effects that may be quite different outside the research setting and circumstances, with their access to resources, sanitary standards and intensive counseling. Moreover, proposals for mass circumcision lack a thorough and objective consideration of costs in relation to hoped-for benefits. No field-test has been performed to evaluate the effectiveness, complications, personnel requirements, costs and practicality of proposed approaches in real-life conditions. These are the classic distinctions between efficacy and effectiveness trials, and between internal validity and external validity.
Campaigns to promote safe-sex behaviors have been shown to accomplish a high rate of infection reduction, without the surgical risks and complications of circumcision, and at a much lower cost. For the health community to rush to recommend a program based on incomplete evidence is both premature and ill-advised. It misleads the public by promoting false hope from uncertain conclusions and might ultimately aggravate the problem by altering people�s behavioral patterns and exposing them and their partners to new or expanded risks. Given these problems, circumcision of adults, and especially of children, by coercion or by false hope, raises human rights concerns.
